catalog_quote: [Sipma 1913] 84. In Frisian, stress is generally subject to the same rules as in other Germanic dialects. ... 87. Simple words, i.e. words which are not compound or derivative, have the stress on the first syllable. This does not always apply to words of foreign origin. ... 89. In verbs formed with the prefixes U- [scanned; = bi-], ge-, for-, ont-, to-, and in nouns or adjectives derived from such words, the stress falls on the second syllable, i. e. on the first syllable of the simple word. ... 92. For compound words it is not possible to give distinct and simple rules. Some have the stress on the first, others on the second element. [Visser & Weening 2015] As to the placement of primary stress in loanwords - which count as monomorphemic words - certain generalizations hold. Since these loanwords enter Frisian via Dutch, the generalizations pertaining to the Dutch stress system also hold f…

sources.citation: Köhnlein, Björn. 2015. Quantity-sensitivity in Dutch. Taalportaal, Dutch Phonology, v1.0 (the page the Frisian 'Quantity-sensitivity' link resolves to).https://taalportaal.org/taalportaal/topic/pid/topic-14020545841908341
sources.quote: 'The question as to whether Dutch stress is quantity-sensitive is under debate in the literature, as many of the data in favor of quantity-sensitivity are not exceptionless. Furthermore, stress in Dutch is at least partly lexical' - the Frisian loan stratum inherits this system, so a hedged QS coding is the faithful one.

sources.citation: Visser, Willem & Joke Weening. 2015. Diachronic aspects of stress (native words vs. loanwords). Taalportaal, Frisian Phonology, v1.0 (December 2015).https://taalportaal.org/taalportaal/topic/pid/topic-14020545839609793
sources.quote: 'Primary word stress in Frisian occurs in three different patterns: a) a Germanic pattern, with stress on the initial stressable syllable, b) a French pattern, with stress on the final stressable syllable, and c) a Latin pattern, with stress on the penultimate syllable (or on the antepenultimate if the penultimate in the source language is light...). All syllables with a full vowel are stressable, whereas schwa syllables cannot be stressed.' 'Since words of Germanic origin usually contain only one full vowel, stress always falls on the syllable containing the full vowel.' 'In Latin loanwords .

sources.citation: Visser, Willem & Joke Weening. 2015. Lexical stress. Taalportaal, Frisian Phonology, v1.0 (December 2015).https://taalportaal.org/taalportaal/topic/pid/topic-14020545890682755
sources.quote: 'Despite the possibility of formulating generalizations concerning the locus of primary stress ..., a variety of cases remain for which these generalizations do not hold. The locus of stress, then, may be a lexical property of words' (kanon /ka.'non/ cannon vs /'ka.non/ canon; tapir vs klavier; kompas vs kanvas etc.).

sources.quote: Instrumental (F0 alignment) study; takes lexical stress position as given, using trisyllabic Frisian words with initial, penultimate and ultimate stress (e.g. 'Anneke bedriget Kornelis'); states no stress-assignment rule. Only instrumental prosody work on West Frisian word-level prominence found via Crossref; no JIPA Illustration of West Frisian exists (only Saterland Frisian 2017, Fering 2004).

tone.summary: Treated as a non-tonal (intonation-only) variety: post-lexical pitch accents (H*L etc.) on stressed syllables plus boundary tones; no lexical tone.

This chapter gives an overview of the lexical tone accent systems that are found in languages of both groups..
